title: Fair-trade coffee: minimum price, premium, the 2001 price crisis and limits of the label

sources.title: Giovannucci D., Liu P. & Byers A. (2008) Adding Value: Certified Coffee Trade in North America, chapter 3 (Certified coffee)
Ronchi L. (2006) “Fairtrade” and Market Failures in Agricultural Commodity Markets. Policy Research Working Paper 4011

sources.publisher: University of Minnesota (copy of FLO standards document)
sources.title: Fairtrade Labelling Organizations International: Fairtrade Standards for Coffee (version January 2003)

sources.publisher: Columbia Business School (Chazen Web Journal of International Business)
sources.title: Zehner D.C. (2002) An Economic Assessment of “Fair Trade” in Coffee

facts.text: Small family farms grow more than 70 percent of the world’s coffee.
Conventional coffee markets are highly competitive, and coffee prices usually move up and down in cycles.
In October 2001 the world market price of coffee fell to a record low of US$0.45 (45 cents) per pound; the price crisis caused great hardship for small coffee growers across the developing world.
Under Fairtrade rules, buyers may buy only from cooperatively organized groups of small producers, and these groups must be democratically controlled by their members.
The Fairtrade minimum, or floor, price is based on the estimated cost of producing coffee sustainably.
Fair-trade coffee is priced from the market price; the minimum price takes over only when the market price is lower than it.
Fairtrade buyers commit to long-term, stable trading relationships with producer groups.
If producers ask, buyers must pay in advance up to 60 percent of the contract value, giving farmers credit against future sales.
The Fairtrade premium is meant for social and economic investment at the level of the cooperative and its community, not for individual farmers.
Members of the producer organization decide democratically how the premium is used.
Producer groups typically spend the premium on building the organization, social programs, services for members, infrastructure projects and quality programs.
In the October 2001 crisis, the price of fair-trade coffee was 180 percent higher than the market price.
When market prices are well above the minimum, the fair-trade price advantage becomes small, and some producers question whether certification is still worth it.
Certified groups can produce far more Fairtrade coffee than the Fairtrade market buys (excess capacity of about 80 percent, Giovannucci et al. 2003), so they also sell to conventional markets.

A study by Mendoza (2000) of Nicaraguan coffee sold in the United Kingdom in the 1990s (1996) found growers got only US$0.09 a pound, about 2 percent of the US$4.23 retail premium, while UK distribution took the largest single share, US$1.54 (36 percent).
